name: Tomoip
confidence_why: 2 read source(s) support the record, but its own quotation is not confirmed first-hand
catalog_citation: Barlow, Russell & Don Killian. 2023. Tomoip phonetics and phonology. Te Reo: the Journal of the Linguistic Society of New Zealand 66(1): 60-96. (Glottolog lists the year as 2024; the PDF title page is dated November 2023.) Corroborated by Barlow, Russell. 2024. Tomoip morphological sketch. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 42: 41-94, p. 42.
catalog_locator: Section 5 'Stress and suprasegmental features', journal p. 80; corroborating line at Barlow 2024 p. 42
catalog_quote: There is no phonemic tone in the language, nor are there other phonemic suprasegmental distinctions. Stress is realized in isolated words by a slight increase in loudness, vowel duration, and pitch. However, lexical stress does not carry a high functional load in the language. There are no known instances in which stress is contrastive. Generally, words tend to receive penultimate stress, although there are exceptions to this tendency. Thus we tentatively hypothesize that Tomoip exhibits non-phonemic penultimate stress. Whereas prefixes such as class prefixes, the causative prefix βa-, and the prefixes me- and te- carry stress when affixed to monosyllabic bases, proclitics such as number markers and subject markers do not. Similarly to prefixes, suffixes such as transitive markers and direct possession markers count as part of the phonological word for purposes of stress assignment. Thus, a shift in stress can be observed, for example, between delkua-n ‘his/her neck’ [ˈdɛl.kuan] and delkua-ʝo ‘my neck’ [dɛlˈkua.ʝo]. Although we are unable at this point to describe Tomoip stress in great detail, we note that this general pattern of penultimate stress (with exceptions) is not uncommon among the languages of the area.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; affixes (prefixes and suffixes, e.g. possessive and transitive suffixes) count toward the word so stress shifts rightward under suffixation (delkua-n [ˈdɛl.kuan] vs delkua-ʝo [dɛlˈkua.ʝo]); proclitics (number and subject markers) are outside the stress domain. Authors call the analysis tentative and note unspecified exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: Authors state there are exceptions to the penultimate tendency but do not list them; proclitics do not count for stress; the possessive preposition e can bear stress as a separate word (Barlow 2024). No phonemic tone, no contrastive length.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word including affixes but excluding proclitics; realization described for isolated (citation-form) words. Corroborated by Barlow 2024 LLM 42 p. 42: 'Stress is generally penultimate, with affixes but not clitics counting for purposes of stress assignment.'
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Tomoip (tqp, tomo1244) as spoken by a consultant born in Milim village, Pomio District, East New Britain; same variety as the Glottolog languoid, no dialect split noted.

Adds the detail that stress is non-contrastive, that affixes count but proclitics do not, and that there is no phonemic tone or vowel length.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (non-contrastive, with unspecified exceptions). Prefixes and suffixes (class prefixes, causative βa-, me-, te-, transitive markers, direct-possession suffixes) are part of the stress domain, so stress shifts under suffixation (delkua-n [ˈdɛl.kuan] 'his/her neck' vs delkua-ʝo [dɛlˈkua.ʝo] 'my neck'); proclitics (number markers, subject markers) are outside the domain and do not carry stress. No phonemic tone, no phonemic vowel length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Phonetic transcriptions of compound-like possessive phrases show two primary marks (ŋom tan 'his/her eye' [ˈŋɔmˈtan], lem tan [ˈlɛmˈtan], p. 80), i.e. each phonological word is stressed separately.
new_statements.exceptions: Authors call the penultimate pattern a tendency with unspecified 'exceptions' and label the analysis tentative ('we are unable at this point to describe Tomoip stress in great detail'; the conclusion, p. 92, lists stress as 'a topic in need of further investigation'). Proclitics do not count for stress assignment; affixes do.
new_statements.identity_note: The description is of Tomoip as spoken in Pomio District, East New Britain (with a small population in Talasea District, West New Britain); no dialect split is described. Footnote 34 (p. 80) concerns Sulka, a neighbouring non-Austronesian language, not Tomoip.
